newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE says Ecu future may be 'right' EMU benchmark.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE says Ecu future may be 'right' EMU benchmark.

text.p: LIFFE's Ecu interest rate future offers practical advantages over Euromarks as the benchmark euro interest rate contract after European currency union takes place, a LIFFE official said on Tuesday.

Giuliano Gregorio, director of business development for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), said it was looking at ways of linking the two contracts, with a spread trading facility being one possibility.
"From a certain point of view that (the Ecu) will be the 'right' contract specification. The market will decide of course, but at least they have this opportunity," he said in an interview.
LIFFE listed its June 1999 Ecu interest rate future on Tuesday, following a listing earlier this year of the first Ecu contract to be traded after the planned 1999 EMU start date.

Interest rate futures, which give an indication of underlying interest rates, are usually traded in values of one million and tick sizes of 25. Euromarks for example, are traded in values of 1.0 million marks and tick sizes of 25 marks.
It has already been decided that Ecus will be converted into euros on a one-for-one basis but the rate at which the mark is fixed against the euro still has to be determined.
"In the Euromark (tick) will still be 25 deutschmarks but 25 deutschmarks will mean something like 49.325 euro," Gregorio said.
"You might have some very odd numbers there which you may want to get rid of by changing your position from the deutschmark contract into the euro contract," he said.
He added it might not be possible to list a Euromark contract after 2002 when sovereign currencies are set to disappear.

"Theoretically the deustchmark will not be the legal contract in Germany. Our members, at a certain stage after EMU happens, may want to move their positions from the Euromark contract into the euro," he said.
"We are looking into mechanisms to facilitate this," he said. He added a normal spread trading facility between the Euromark and euro would be one option.
"It might be that EMU happens but market participants will decide to stick to the Euromark. It depends on what kind of confidence they have that euro is a good thing,"
Peter Osler, head of research at leading brokerage GNI in London, said he expected Euromarks to hold sway.

"It's normally the one that gets taken on first is the one that people use," he said. "I can't see any reason why people would stop using the Euromark to speculate on rates in monetary union if it goes ahead." --Jacqueline Thorpe, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
